title: Exploring Antitrust and Platform Power in Generative AI
venue: Workshop on Generative AI and Law, co-located with the International Conference on Machine Learning
extended_summary:
This paper examines antitrust and platform power in the generative AI ecosystem, focusing on whether a small number of large technology companies are becoming dominant across the data, talent, compute, infrastructure, and model layers of the generative AI stack. It argues that the same incumbent firms that already hold power in search, cloud, hardware, and digital advertising may be carrying that advantage into generative AI, reinforcing concentration rather than enabling open competition.

The paper does not study an educational intervention, AI tool deployment in schools, or any learner population. Instead, it provides a legal-economic analysis of market structure, vertical integration, and barriers to entry, drawing on examples such as proprietary data access, expensive model training, human feedback labor, and dependence on proprietary cloud and hardware infrastructure. It also discusses how current and emerging regulation, including the EU AI Act, could shape market dynamics.

Its main conclusion is that generative AI is likely to remain concentrated among highly resourced incumbent firms because training frontier models requires large-scale data, financing, infrastructure, and human expertise. The paper suggests that open-sourcing alone is unlikely to solve these structural inequities and calls for future quantitative work on market definition, substitutability, and access conditions in specific generative AI markets.
quality_tier_rationale: This is a conceptual/argumentative article in antitrust law and platform power, not an empirical education study. It contains no causal design, no K-12 sample, and no intervention/outcome measurement relevant to the requested evidence filter.
impact_tier_rationale: No educational effect is estimated, so there is no measurable instructional impact to assess. The paper offers no evidence that could sustain the optimistic thesis about AI tools improving scientific reasoning or inquiry in K-12 settings.

finding.finding_summary: This is a theoretical/legal analysis of market dominance in generative AI, not a K-12 causal comparison study of AI for scientific reasoning or inquiry. It does not report delayed post-tests, transfer tasks, subgroup effects, or implementation fidelity because it does not evaluate an educational intervention at all.
finding.measure: Legal-economic analysis of market structure, antitrust theory, and platform power
